messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# James

James was thirty-eight when the police stopped him. He'd been driving the same bus route for twelve years—the 7 AM crosstown that picked up shift workers, students, and regulars he'd come to know by sight. He was respected on that route, the kind of driver who waited for the elderly woman with the walker, who knew which passengers preferred the back seat. On a Tuesday morning in March, he was pulled over by two state troopers while parked at the downtown terminal. They said there had been a report—a passenger complaint about suspicious behavior. James was confused; he'd done nothing wrong. The officers approached with hands near their belts, voices clipped and authoritative. One demanded his license and registration. The other stood at the passenger window, watching him. James's hands shook as he reached for the glove compartment. The officer at his window suddenly shouted, "Keep your hands visible!" James froze. What followed was a search of his vehicle, aggressive questioning, and a pat-down conducted in front of his coworkers and a gathering of passengers. The complaint turned out to be baseless—a misunderstanding, a case of mistaken identity. The officers apologized, almost perfunctorily, and left. But something in James had fractured that morning. He felt exposed, humiliated, and for the first time in his life, he understood that his presence alone could be interpreted as a threat.

In the months that followed, James began to notice things he'd never paid attention to before. Police cars on the street made his chest tighten. If he saw an officer at a bus stop, his palms would sweat. The memory of that morning—the officer's shout, the feeling of being trapped in his own vehicle—would surface without warning, often at the worst moments: mid-route, surrounded by passengers, unable to escape. When the memory came, his body would flood with adrenaline, and he'd grip the steering wheel so hard his knuckles went white. To manage these moments, James had developed a habit of turning up the radio or the in-cabin audio system, flooding the space with noise and distraction. The loudness helped push the memory away, at least temporarily, though it left him feeling raw and exhausted.

Over time, James's understanding of the world had shifted in ways he couldn't quite articulate. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous—that authority figures, even those meant to protect, could turn on you without cause. The police had shown him that. This conviction had begun to seep into his thinking about people more broadly. If the police couldn't be trusted, who could? His coworkers, once friendly, now felt like potential witnesses to his humiliation. His sister, who worked in city administration, suddenly seemed complicit in a system that had wronged him. He had largely withdrawn from the community center where he'd once played basketball on weekends, telling himself it wasn't safe anymore, though what exactly he feared remained vague. The loss felt profound—he'd lost not just his sense of safety but his sense of belonging.

This erosion of trust fed his avoidance. When passengers tried to engage him in conversation, James would keep his eyes forward, offering only curt responses. When he thought about attending his nephew's school event or going to the local diner where he used to meet friends, he'd find reasons not to go. He avoided people, period. The thought of being around others, of being seen, had become intolerable. His apartment had become his refuge, though even there he wasn't at peace. He'd begun checking the locks obsessively—the front door, the back door, the windows—sometimes five or six times an evening. His mind wouldn't settle. At work, he found it harder to concentrate on the road; his thoughts scattered between hypervigilance and dread. When passengers asked him questions, he'd snap at them, irritable and sharp in ways that surprised even him. One regular, an elderly man he'd chatted with for years, asked if he was okay. James nearly bit his head off, then felt a wave of shame that made him want to hide.

The avoidance and isolation had created a vicious loop. The less he engaged with people, the more his conviction that they couldn't be trusted seemed confirmed. The more he believed the world was dangerous, the more he retreated, checked his locks, turned up the noise. And each time he encountered a police car, or someone mentioned authority, or he caught sight of a uniform, the memory would crash through again, sending him scrambling for his maladaptive strategies—the music, the isolation, the hiding. By the time James finally called a therapist, he'd been on medical leave from his job for two weeks. His supervisor had suggested it gently, noting that passengers had complained about his behavior, that he seemed "on edge." James knew he was falling apart. What terrified him most wasn't just the memory of that morning, but the person he was becoming—isolated, angry, trapped in a cage of his own making. He desperately wanted to believe that people were trustworthy again, that he could return to his bus route and his life. But right now, the thought of facing either felt impossible.
